question: The magnetic field strength inside a current carrying solenoid is:

options.text: more at ends and less at centre
less at ends and more at centre

solution:
The correct answer is __**uniform and non-zero**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The magnetic field strength inside a current carrying solenoid is uniform and non-zero.
 
• A solenoid is a long coil of wire wound in the form of a helix, and when an electric current passes through it, a magnetic field is generated.
 
• Inside the solenoid, the magnetic field lines are parallel and evenly spaced, indicating a uniform field.
 
• The strength of the magnetic field inside the solenoid is given by the formula: B = μ₀nI, Where: B is the magnetic field, μ₀ is the permeability of free space, n is the number of turns per unit length, and I is the current.
 
• This uniform magnetic field is a result of the superposition of the magnetic fields created by each turn of the wire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **At the ends of the solenoid,** the magnetic field lines start to spread out, causing the field to become weaker and less uniform.
 
• Outside the solenoid, the magnetic field is much weaker compared to the inside.
 
• Solenoids are widely used in various applications such as electromagnets, inductors, and transformers.
 
• The concept of a solenoid is fundamental in electromagnetism and is essential for understanding the behavior of magnetic fields in different configurations.
